name: Apple App Store
tagline: Apple's editorial Today feed and web catalog of iOS, iPadOS and macOS apps
description: The public web front of Apple's App Store. The bare domain redirects to /us/iphone/today, an editorially curated feed of app and game features, and the top nav splits into Today, Games, Apps and Arcade across the iPhone, iPad, Mac, Vision, Watch and TV platforms. For this catalog its only real use is as a directory: you can find real shipping apps to study, read their product pages, and look at icon art, screenshot sets and listing copy. It holds no developer documentation, no Human Interface Guidelines and no downloadable design assets.
agent_guidance: Do not treat this as a design resource — it is a consumer storefront and the root URL lands on rotating editorial content that will not match what you saw yesterday. Reach for it only to confirm that a named iOS app exists, to read its listing, or to grab screenshots of a competitor for reference; use the iTunes Search API (itunes.apple.com/search) rather than scraping these pages. For actual iOS design rules go to Apple's Human Interface Guidelines instead, and for app UI patterns go to a screen gallery like Mobbin.
why_it_matters: It is the canonical registry of what actually shipped on Apple platforms, which makes it a fact-checking source rather than an inspiration source.
evidence: https://apps.apple.com (302 to https://apps.apple.com/us/iphone/today), raw HTML inspected

name: Awwwards
tagline: Juried web design awards with a filterable archive of sites by category and tech stack
description: Awwwards judges submitted websites and gives out Site of the Day, Site of the Month, Site of the Year, Honorable Mention and Developer awards. The /websites/ archive is the useful part for build work: every entry is tagged by industry category (31 of them, from Portfolio and E-commerce to Experimental and Real Estate), by style tag (Parallax, Microinteractions, Horizontal Layout, Infinite Scroll and about 45 more), and by the technology that built it (over 110 tags including Three.js, GSAP, Webflow, Framer, Next.js, Locomotive Scroll, Lottie and WebGL). Around it sit a Directory of 6,064 agencies and professionals, an Academy of paid courses, a Market of paid templates and assets, plus Jobs, Blog and Conferences.
pricing_detail: Browsing is free. Market items observed at $49-$79 USD. Pro membership, site submissions, Academy courses and Conference tickets are paid; exact tiers not verified.
agent_guidance: Use the technology filter, not the front page — /websites/?tech=gsap or ?tech=threejs is the fastest way to find real, shipped examples of a specific stack, and each entry names its full tool chain, which is rare. Be aware of the bias: this archive rewards award-bait marketing sites with heavy WebGL, custom cursors and scroll hijacking, so it is a poor reference for dense product UI, dashboards or accessibility work. Pair it with a screen gallery (Mobbin, Godly) for product surfaces, and never quote an Awwwards site as an accessibility precedent.
why_it_matters: It is the longest-running juried gallery of high-craft web work, and its per-entry technology tagging turns it into a searchable index of which stack produced which effect.

name: Antalik React Effects
tagline: npm workspaces monorepo shipping border-beam and liquid-gooey React effect packages
description: The repo behind Jakub Antalik's React effect packages. The URL /Jakubantalik/border-beam now redirects to /Jakubantalik/Libraries, an npm-workspaces monorepo that publishes two zero-dependency packages plus the demo site for each. border-beam renders an animated traveling or breathing glow around any wrapped element; liquid-gooey (v0.1.0) does SVG-filter gooey merge, jelly shape change, contact dissolve and liquid-rubber trail effects, and claims Safari support. Each package carries its own README and MIT LICENSE, and releases publish per package from a GitHub release.
install: npm install border-beam   # or: npm install liquid-gooey
agent_guidance: Read the package README at packages/<name>/README.md, not the repo root — the root README only documents the workspace layout and deploy setup. Both packages are zero-dependency with react/react-dom >=18 as the only peers, so they drop into a shadcn/Tailwind project without pulling in framer-motion or GSAP. Note the versions differ sharply in maturity: border-beam is at 1.3.0 and stable, liquid-gooey is at 0.1.0 and its SVG-filter approach is far more expensive to composite, so do not put many gooey instances on one screen.
why_it_matters: A rare pair of effect packages that ship as real npm libraries with zero dependencies instead of copy-paste snippets, and the author documents the browser-support and performance trade-offs honestly.
evidence: https://github.com/Jakubantalik/border-beam (301 to /Jakubantalik/Libraries), api.github.com/repos/Jakubantalik/Libraries, raw README.md, raw packages/border-beam/README.md, registry.npmjs.org/border-beam, registry.npmjs.org/liquid-gooey

name: Border Beam
tagline: React component that draws an animated traveling or breathing glow around any element
description: Border Beam is a single zero-dependency React component, published to npm as border-beam (v1.3.0, MIT). You wrap any element in <BorderBeam> and it overlays an animated glow, auto-detecting the child's border-radius. Five size presets split into two families: rotate (sm, md, line) drives a conic-gradient beam masked to the border via CSS @property keyframes, and pulse (pulse-inner, pulse-outside) breathes from a single shared frame-rate-capped requestAnimationFrame loop that writes plain CSS custom properties. Four color variants (colorful, mono, ocean, sunset), three themes (dark, light, auto), plus strength, duration, brightness, saturation, hueRange, staticColors, borderRadius, active and onActivate/onDeactivate callbacks. This site is the live demo; it is a Vite SPA whose served HTML is an empty shell.
agent_guidance: Reach for this instead of hand-rolling a Magic-UI-style border beam: it is a real npm package with zero dependencies and react>=18 as its only peer, so it composes with shadcn/ui and Tailwind without adding framer-motion. Two traps are documented and both bite: pulse-outside renders behind the child at z-index -1 and needs an opaque child plus overflow room in the parent, and it borrows the child's own 1px border as the idle hairline, so give the child a border or an inset box-shadow. Also gate the rotate presets yourself — only the pulse presets ship a prefers-reduced-motion block — and expect stepped rather than smooth motion on browsers without CSS @property (pre-Chrome 85, pre-Safari 15.4, pre-Firefox 128).
why_it_matters: The glowing-border effect is everywhere in AI product UI and is usually copy-pasted badly; this packages it properly, with reduced-motion handling, a shared rAF loop and honest degradation notes.
notable_for: 5 presets across rotate and pulse families
evidence: https://beam.jakubantalik.com (200, 3.4KB Vite shell + meta tags, /assets/main-CHM1__fq.js inspected), raw packages/border-beam/README.md, registry.npmjs.org/border-beam

name: Jakub Antalik
tagline: Portfolio of a product designer working on interaction and motion, Design Lead at Fun.xyz
description: Personal site of Jakub Antalik, a product designer focused on interaction and motion. He is Design Lead at Fun.xyz, with prior work at 0x.org, Frame.io (acquired by Adobe) and Intercom. The site is a single page of selected work with live, customizable demos embedded in it, and it doubles as the hub for his open-source releases: Transitions.dev, Border Beam, Liquid Gooey and Liquid Metal. Contact and profile links to X, GitHub, Instagram and LinkedIn are listed at the bottom.
agent_guidance: Treat this as an index page, not a resource: the value is the four projects it points at, so follow them directly — transitions.dev for copy-paste web-app transitions, beam.jakubantalik.com and npm border-beam for the animated border glow, gooey.jakubantalik.com and npm liquid-gooey for SVG-filter gooey effects, and metal.jakubantalik.com for a WebGL chrome shader on buttons. Only border-beam and liquid-gooey are published npm packages; the other two are copy-paste or demo-only, so do not write an install command for them. Also study the page itself if you are building a motion portfolio — the demos are interactive and customizable inline rather than video captures.
why_it_matters: One designer who both ships production motion work and releases the underlying effects as maintained MIT packages, which makes the portfolio a reliable pointer to real, usable code.
evidence: https://jakubantalik.com, plus status/title checks of https://transitions.dev, https://metal.jakubantalik.com, https://gooey.jakubantalik.com (all 200)

It was saved under design-reference tags, which suggests visual design inspiration, but nothing about the post itself has been verified. agent_guidance: Do not fetch this URL — Instagram serves a login wall to unauthenticated clients and any content you infer from the slug is a guess. If you need the post, go through an authenticated Instagram tool or ask the user for a screenshot. A single social post is inspiration at best; never cite it as a source for a pattern, a spec or a component API.
why_it_matters: It is a saved visual reference with no verifiable content, kept in the index only as a pointer back to the user's own bookmark.
